key_concept: Grignard reagents are strong bases, so any compound with an acidic hydrogen (on O, N or S, or a terminal alkyne C–H) protonates the carbanion part and gives the corresponding hydrocarbon.
steps: In cyclohexylmagnesium bromide, $C_6H_{11}MgBr$, the C–Mg bond is highly polar. The cyclohexyl carbon behaves as a carbanion ($C_6H_{11}^-$), which is a very strong base.
Cyclohexylamine, $C_6H_{11}NH_2$, has acidic N–H hydrogens (p$K_a \approx 35$). These are far more acidic than the C–H of cyclohexane (p$K_a \approx 50$).
An acid–base reaction therefore occurs before any substitution can happen: $C_6H_{11}MgBr + C_6H_{11}NH_2 \rightarrow C_6H_{12} + C_6H_{11}NHMgBr$.
The carbanion picks up $H^+$ from N and becomes cyclohexane, $C_6H_{12}$. The amine is converted into a magnesium amide salt.
Of the products formed, only cyclohexane appears among the options.
why_not_others: The $NH_2$ group is a very poor leaving group, so the Grignard reagent cannot displace it to form a C–C bond (bicyclohexyl) or a C–N bond (dicyclohexylamine). It also cannot substitute on a ring C–H to give the $NH_2$-bearing bicyclohexyl. Simple deprotonation of the N–H is the only reaction that takes place.
common_trap: Treating the Grignard reagent as a nucleophile that couples with the amine, giving dicyclohexylamine or bicyclohexyl, instead of recognising the fast acid–base reaction with the N–H hydrogen.
time_saving_tip: Whenever RMgX meets a compound containing O–H, N–H, S–H or a terminal $\equiv C$–H, write R–H straight away; here R–H is cyclohexane.
